title: Knowledge check: Hypothesis Testing

questions.prompt: For “Hypothesis Testing”, which approach best supports a reliable result?
options: Inspect assumptions, run a small example, and verify an edge case.
Trust the first output without inspecting its inputs.
Hide warnings and skip validation to make the result look clean.
Change several unrelated parts at once so the cause of any result is unclear.
questions.answer_key: Inspect assumptions, run a small example, and verify an edge case.
questions.explanation: A test result depends on the question, design, assumptions and uncertainty; it does not by itself measure importance. Reliable work makes assumptions visible and checks behavior before scaling up.

questions.prompt: Which item is explicitly listed under “Hypothesis Testing” in the source curriculum?
options: Change unrelated settings before checking the input
Assume one example proves every edge case
Skip validation when the output looks plausible
questions.explanation: The source PDF lists “Null and Alternative Hypotheses” as part of lesson 145. The lesson retains the original topic wording.

questions.prompt: When applying “Hypothesis Testing” to real work, what should you do before relying on the result?
options: Validate inputs and output shape, test a boundary case, and state limitations.
Assume missing and malformed inputs never occur.
Use the same method regardless of data type or the research question.
Remove inconvenient observations without recording the decision.
questions.answer_key: Validate inputs and output shape, test a boundary case, and state limitations.
questions.explanation: State the null hypothesis, test assumptions, and write a conclusion in the study context. Record assumptions and known limitations instead of presenting a demonstration as proof.
